 9   Q6.   WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR REBUTTAL TESTIMONY?

10   A.    The purpose of my rebuttal testimony is to respond to various adjustments to EPE’s

11         rate base and cost of service proposed by New Mexico Public Regulation

12         Commission ("NMPRC") Staff witnesses Jonah B. Mauldin and Naomi Velasquez,

13         City of Las Cruces and Doña Ana County ("CLC/DAC") witness Mark E. Garrett,

 2   Q10. ARE THERE OTHER ITEMS INCLUDED IN WORKPAPER A-3,

 3        ADJUSTMENT NO. 13 THAT ARE ADDRESSED BY OTHER EPE

 4        WITNESSES?

 6        asset and unrecovered costs associated with legacy meters. EPE witness Cynthia S.

 7        Prieto addresses the Staff and intervenor recommendations related to those items,

13   Q11. WHY DOES EPE DISAGREE WITH CLC/DAC’S PROPOSED FIVE-YEAR

14        AMORTIZATION PERIOD?

15   A.   Although EPE recognizes the importance of mitigating customer rate impacts, a

16        five-year amortization period would unnecessarily extend the recovery of costs

17        EPE has already incurred and deferred. Because EPE has already incurred and

18        financed these costs and experienced regulatory lag before recovery begins,

19        extending the amortization period to five years would further delay recovery of

20        those costs. EPE originally proposed a two-year amortization period but is willing

21        to accept a three-year period, consistent with the recommendations of Staff and


                                                5
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                      JULISSA I. REZA

 1        NMSU witnesses. A three-year period is superior for two reasons. First, a three-

 2        year period better matches the expected period that the rates set in this case will be

 3        in effect, so that the customers who benefit from these deferred costs are the

 4        customers who pay for them. A three-year amortization period also more properly

 5        reflects the timing of EPE's planned rate case filings, as discussed in the rebuttal

 6        testimony of EPE witness George Novela. Second, a three-year amortization period

 7        represents a reasonable compromise that balances EPE’s timely recovery of

 8        prudently incurred costs against customer impact, whereas a five-year period

 9        increases the risk that recovery extends beyond the period these rates are in effect

10        and defers cost recovery EPE has already financed. Accordingly, EPE does not

11        believe extending the recovery period to five years is warranted.

12

13   Q12. DOES M. GARRETT OFFER ANY PRINCIPLED BASIS FOR SELECTING

14        FIVE YEARS RATHER THAN THREE?

15   A.   No. Mr. Garrett selects five years primarily to reduce the near-term revenue

16        requirement, not because five years corresponds to the nature or useful life of these

17        deferred costs (M. Garrett Direct at 66-67).

18

19                                   B. CARRYING COSTS

20   Q13. DOES STAFF PROPOSE AN ADJUSTMENT TO THE CARRYING COSTS




                                                6
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                      JULISSA I. REZA

 1        ASSOCIATED WITH EPE'S REGULATORY ASSETS?

 2   A.   Yes. Staff witness Mauldin recommends that the Commission deny EPE's

 3        requested carrying costs associated with the EIM and AMS TVRPP regulatory

 4        assets. He states that the Commission did not expressly authorize carrying costs for

 5        either regulatory asset and that the deferred costs are O&M in nature (Mauldin

 6        Direct at 14-15).

 7

 8   Q14. DO YOU AGREE WITH STAFF’S RECOMMENDATION REGARDING

 9        CARRYING COSTS ON THE EIM AND TVRPP REGULATORY ASSETS?

10   A.   Yes. For purposes of this case only, EPE is willing to accept Staff witness

11        Mauldin’s recommendation and will not seek carrying costs on the EIM or AMS

12        TVRPP regulatory assets. The carrying costs included in EPE’s original request

13        were approximately $93,022 for the EIM regulatory asset and $14,078 for the AMS

14        TVRPP regulatory asset. However, EPE’s acceptance of this adjustment should

15        not be interpreted as agreement with Staff’s broader position that carrying costs are

16        categorically inappropriate because the Commission did not expressly authorize

17        carrying costs when the regulatory assets were established or because the deferred

18        costs were originally O&M expenses.

19

20   Q15. WHY DOES EPE DISAGREE WITH STAFF’S BROADER POSITION

21        REGARDING CARRYING COSTS ON DEFERRED REGULATORY


                                                7
                                EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                     JULISSA I. REZA

 1        COSTS?

 2   A.   EPE believes the appropriateness of carrying costs should be evaluated based on

 3        the facts and circumstances applicable to the particular regulatory asset. When

 4        recovery of incurred costs is deferred, EPE must finance those costs until they are

 5        recovered from customers, and carrying costs recognize that financing period. The

 6        fact that the underlying costs originated as O&M expenses does not, by itself,

 7        eliminate the financing cost associated with deferring recovery. Moreover, New

 8        Mexico ratemaking precedent demonstrates that carrying costs may be recognized

 9        on deferred regulatory costs. For example, in Case No. 15-00127-UT, EPE sought

10        recovery of deferred Renewable Portfolio Standard costs with carrying costs based

11        on the weighted average cost of capital established in that proceeding. EPE

12        subsequently identified its New Mexico Renewable Energy Cost regulatory asset

13        as including Renewable Energy Portfolio compliance expenses and associated

14        carrying costs. Therefore, although EPE is not seeking carrying costs on the EIM

15        and AMS TVRPP regulatory assets in this case, EPE does not believe its acceptance

16        of Staff’s adjustment should establish a broader principle regarding the

17        appropriateness of carrying costs on deferred regulatory costs in future

18        proceedings.

19

20   Q16. DOES STAFF OPPOSE CARRYING COSTS ON ALL OF EPE'S

21        REGULATORY ASSETS?


                                               8
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                      JULISSA I. REZA

 1   A.   No. Staff does not recommend disallowing the carrying costs associated with EPE's

 2        Final Order on Remand regulatory asset because Staff states that those carrying

 3        costs were expressly authorized by the Commission (Mauldin Direct at 16). Staff's

 4        proposed disallowance is limited to the EIM and AMS TVRPP regulatory assets.

 5        Staff’s willingness to allow carrying costs on the Remand asset confirms that the

 6        question is one of specific authorization and financing, not a categorical bar on

 7        carrying costs for deferred costs.

 9                           IV.    RATE CASE EXPENSES

10   Q17. WHAT ADJUSTMENTS DID STAFF AND CLC/DAC PROPOSE TO EPE'S

11        RATE CASE EXPENSES?

12   A.   Staff witness Velasquez recommends a 50 percent disallowance of EPE's requested

13        rate case expense through a 50/50 ratepayer/shareholder cost-sharing mechanism,

14        reducing the recoverable amount from $2,015,800 to $1,007,900. (Velasquez

15        Direct at 7-9.) CLC/DAC witness Garrett recommends limiting recoverable rate

16        case expense to $1.630 million, excluding these rate case expenses from rate base,

17        and amortizing these rate case expenses over a five-year period and establishing a

18        regulatory liability if another rate case does not occur before the recoverable

19        balance has been fully amortized. (M. Garrett Direct at 49.) EPE’s revised rate case

20        expense treatment is reflected in Exhibit JIR-2R, Workpaper A-3, Adjustment No.

21        10-Regulatory Commission Expense.


                                               9
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                      JULISSA I. REZA

 1

 2   Q18. MS. VELASQUEZ RELIES ON A LAW REVIEW ARTICLE, ATTACHED

 3        AS HER EXHIBIT NAV-2, TO SUPPORT STAFF’S 50/50 COST-SHARING

 4        RECOMMENDATION. HAVE YOU REVIEWED THAT ARTICLE?

 5   A.   Yes. Exhibit NAV-2 is an appendix from the Energy Law Journal (Vol. 46.3:571

 6        (2025)) that surveys how utility regulators in all fifty states, the District of

 7        Columbia, and Puerto Rico treat recovery of utility rate case expense. While Ms.

 8        Velasquez cites the article’s description of New Jersey to support a 50/50 sharing

 9        mechanism, the article as a whole demonstrates that New Jersey’s approach is the

10        exception, not the rule, and that New Mexico follows the predominant approach of

11        allowing a utility to recover its prudently incurred rate case expense.

12

13   Q19. PLEASE EXPLAIN WHY NEW JERSEY IS AN EXCEPTION.

14   A.   According to Exhibit NAV-2, New Jersey limits a utility to recovering only “half

15        of their rate case expenses.” The article further explains that “[t]here is no specific

16        regulatory or statutory provision governing this practice in New Jersey.” Rather, it

17        is a policy the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities adopted through its own

18        decisions beginning in the early 1980s. (Exhibit NAV-2 at 606.) In other words,

19        New Jersey’s 50/50 sharing mechanism rests on that state board’s policy

20        preference, not on any statute, regulation, or broadly accepted ratemaking principle,

21        and the survey does not identify any other state that imposes a comparable across-


                                                10
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                      JULISSA I. REZA

 1        the-board 50 percent disallowance of otherwise-prudent rate case expense.

 2

 3   Q20. DOES THE ARTICLE SHOW THAT OTHER STATES HAVE REJECTED

 4        THE NEW JERSEY SHARING APPROACH?

 5   A.   Yes. The same survey reports that the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio

 6        “rejected the argument that utilities should recover only half of their rate case

 7        expenses, i.e., ‘share’ those expenses between ratepayers and shareholders,”

 8        finding that such a policy “would be contrary to the reasonableness standard.”

 9        (Exhibit NAV-2 at 611 & n.335.) The article thus shows not only that New Jersey’s

10        50/50 approach is an outlier, but that at least one other commission has specifically

11        considered and rejected it.

12

13   Q21. HOW DOES THE ARTICLE DESCRIBE NEW MEXICO’S APPROACH?

14   A.   The article describes New Mexico as a state that “permits utilities to recover

15        prudent rate case expenses amortized over a period of years.” (Exhibit NAV-2 at

16        607.) It explains that, although New Mexico law imposes a heightened burden to

17        demonstrate that rate case expenses are prudent, the New Mexico Supreme Court

18        has held that the Commission “cannot simply deny recovery altogether” where a

19        utility has prudently incurred rate case expense, but instead “must determine the

20        amount of reasonable and prudent rate case expenses incurred by the utility.”

21        (Exhibit NAV-2 at 607–08 & n.310, citing In re PNM Gas Servs., 129 N.M. 1, 26–


                                               11
                                   EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                   REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                        JULISSA I. REZA

 1        27 (2000).) The article also notes that the Commission has been relatively

 2        deferential in applying this standard, recently approving recovery of more than $3.5

 3        million in rate case expense for another New Mexico utility. (Exhibit NAV-2 at 608

 4        & n.311.) New Mexico’s approach is therefore to allow recovery of reasonable and

 5        prudently incurred rate case expense, rather than imposing an across-the-board 50

 6        percent disallowance.

 7

 8   Q22. IS NEW MEXICO’S APPROACH CONSISTENT WITH THE APPROACH

 9        FOLLOWED IN MOST OTHER STATES?

10   A.   Yes. The survey shows that the predominant approach across the states is to permit

11        a utility to recover its actual, reasonable, or prudent rate case expense, amortized

12        over a period of years that approximates the interval between rate cases. States

13        following this general approach in the survey include, for example, Alabama,

14        Alaska, Arkansas, Connecticut, Delaware, New York, North Carolina, Oklahoma,

15        and Rhode Island. New Mexico’s approach is squarely within this mainstream.

16        Staff’s proposed 50/50 disallowance, by contrast, would move New Mexico away

17        from this well-established approach and toward the New Jersey outlier, a result the

18        article’s survey does not support.

19

20   Q23. DOES EPE AGREE WITH THE RECOMMENDED DISALLOWANCES

21        OF RATE CASE EXPENSES?


                                               12
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                      JULISSA I. REZA

 1   A.   No. EPE does not agree with Staff's proposed 50 percent disallowance or

 2        CLC/DAC's proposed limitation of recoverable rate case expense to $1.630 million.

 3        EPE's requested estimated rate case expenses reflect the costs reasonably expected

 4        to be incurred in this proceeding. EPE witness George Novela addresses the nature

 8   Q24. DOES EPE AGREE WITH CLC/DAC’S RECOMMENDATION TO

 9        AMORTIZE RATE CASE EXPENSES OVER A FIVE-YEAR PERIOD?

10   A.   No. EPE does not agree with CLC/DAC’s recommendation related to a five-year

11        amortization period but does agree to a three-year amortization period. Please refer

14   Q25. DOES EPE AGREE WITH CLC/DAC’S RECOMMENDATION TO

15        EXCLUDE RATE CASE EXPENSE FROM RATE BASE?

16   A.   EPE does not object to this recommendation, but it does not require an adjustment.

17        Mr. Garrett recommends excluding rate case expense from rate base. (M. Garrett

21        filed rate base already excludes these amounts, Mr. Garrett's recommendation is

 3   Q26. DOES EPE AGREE WITH CLC/DAC’S RECOMMENDATION TO

 4             ESTABLISH A REGULATORY LIABILITY IF ANOTHER RATE CASE

13        V.     RESPONSE TO STAFF AND INTERVENORS’ DIRECT TESTIMONY

14               RELATED TO DEFERRED BUENA VISTA 1 CAPACITY COSTS AND

15                                           CARRYING COSTS

16                       A. DEFERRED BUENA VISTA 1 CAPACITY COSTS

17   Q27. DO STAFF AND CLC/DAC PROPOSE AN ADJUSTMENT TO EPE'S

18             DEFERRED BUENA VISTA 1 CAPACITY COSTS?

19   A.        Yes. Staff witness Mauldin and CLC/DAC witness Garrett recommend that the

20             Commission deny recovery of EPE's deferred Buena Vista 1 ("BV 1") capacity

21             costs.    Both witnesses rely, in part, on the absence of an accounting order


                                                   14
                                EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                     JULISSA I. REZA

 1        specifically authorizing deferral of those costs. (Mauldin Direct at 12-13; M.

 2        Garrett Direct at 68, 71). Staff also relies on its characterization of the

 3        Commission's treatment of EPE's requested recovery of BV 1 capacity costs in Case

 4        No. 19-00348-UT.

 5

 6   Q28. DO      YOU       AGREE         WITH        STAFF’S        AND       CLC/DAC’S

 7        RECOMMENDATION REGARDING THE DEFERRED BV 1 CAPACITY

 8        COSTS?

 9   A.   No. EPE continues to support recovery of the deferred BV 1 capacity costs. As

10        discussed below, these costs were incurred before the ongoing BV 1 capacity costs

11        could be reflected in base rates, and EPE believes recovery of these deferred costs

12        is appropriate in this proceeding. EPE’s revised treatment of the deferred BV 1

13        capacity costs is reflected in Exhibit JIR-1R, Workpaper A-3, Adjustment No. 2-

14        Fuel and Purchased Power Expense.

15

16   Q29. STAFF CONTENDS THAT EPE CONTROLLED THE TIMING OF ITS

17        RATE CASE AND COULD HAVE SOUGHT RECOVERY EARLIER.

18        HOW DO YOU RESPOND?

19   A.   The Commission directed that BV 1 capacity costs be addressed in EPE’s next base

20        rate case. EPE is doing so in this proceeding. Because the Commission identified

21        the next base rate case as the appropriate forum for recovery of these costs, EPE


                                              15
                                EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                     JULISSA I. REZA

 1        believes that it was reasonable to defer the BV 1 capacity costs incurred in the

 2        interim.

 3

 4   Q30. HOW DID THE COMMISSION PREVIOUSLY ADDRESS RECOVERY OF

 5        BV 1 CAPACITY COSTS?

 6   A.   In Case No. 19-00348-UT, the Commission approved the BV 1 long term –

 7        purchase power agreement. The Commission allowed EPE to recover BV 1 energy

 8        costs through the FPPCAC and directed that recovery of BV 1 capacity costs be

 9        addressed in EPE’s next base rate case, which is this proceeding.              The

10        Commission’s Order states that “EPE is authorized to recover the costs of the solar

11        portion of the amended BV-1-PPA through EPE’s FPPCAC, and to recover the

12        costs of the associated battery storage through base rates.” (Case Nos. 19-00348-

13        UT, Order Adopting Recommended Decision with Modifications at 8, ¶ 25. (May

14        17, 2023))

15

16   Q31. DOES THE ABSENCE OF A SPECIFIC ACCOUNTING ORDER

17        PRECLUDE EPE FROM RECORDING THE BV 1 CAPACITY COSTS AS

18        A REGULATORY ASSET?

19   A.   No. The absence of a separate accounting order does not, by itself, preclude

20        regulatory asset accounting. Under the FERC Uniform System of Accounts

21        (“USoA”), Account 182.3, Other Regulatory Assets, provides for the recording of


                                              16
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                      JULISSA I. REZA

 1       costs that would otherwise be recognized in current-period income when it is

 2       probable that these costs will be included in a different period for purposes of

 3       developing rates. The USoA further contemplates that the Commission will

 4       ultimately determine recoverability because, if recovery of an amount recorded in

 5       Account 182.3 is subsequently disallowed, the amount is charged to expense at that

 6       time.

 7               Here, EPE had a reasonable basis for concluding that regulatory asset

 8       treatment was appropriate. The Commission approved the BV 1 long-term power

 9       purchase agreement, including the resource giving rise to the capacity costs. In

10       addition, as discussed above, the Commission permitted recovery of BV 1 energy

11       costs through the FPPCAC while providing that recovery of the BV 1 capacity costs

12       would be addressed in EPE's next base rate case. Consistent with that treatment,

13       EPE deferred the New Mexico portion of the capacity costs incurred before those

14       costs could be reflected prospectively in base rates and is requesting recovery of

15       that historical balance in this proceeding. Recording these costs as a regulatory asset

16       preserved them for consideration by the Commission in the proceeding in which

17       their recovery was to be addressed; it did not predetermine that the Commission

18       must allow recovery.

19

20   Q32. WOULD RECOVERY OF THE DEFERRED BALANCE RESULT IN

21       CUSTOMERS PAYING TWICE FOR THE SAME CAPACITY COSTS?


                                               17
                                EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                     JULISSA I. REZA

 1   A.   No. EPE's requested amortization relates to capacity costs incurred before the

 2        ongoing annual Buena Vista capacity costs are reflected in rates. EPE proposes to

 3        recover the deferred balance over a three-year amortization period. The historical

 4        deferred balance and the prospective annual capacity costs relate to different

 5        recovery periods and do not represent recovery of the same cost twice.

 7                                B. CARRYING COSTS

 8   Q33. DO YOU AGREE WITH STAFF AND CLC/DAC’S RECOMMENDATION
